tested: Where a later run supersedes an earlier reading, the correction appears as a new dated row that references the original entry; the original is left intact so the development of the investigation stays visible.
notes: Entries before 2026-07-09 predate the deterministic ground-truth methodology adopted later - independent IfcOpenShell verification of every platform claim, a public positive control model (Duplex Apartment, buildingSMART community sample), and explicit recording of hypotheses that were tested and withdrawn. Twenty upstream commits were merged after that point - including 6e56fd8 (writeback unified on a mutation-journal executor), PR #16 (entity-resolver fixes) and 9e82cf4 (RAV benchmark harness and IFC round-trip diff) - and are NOT reflected in these results. title: Entity Description Whitelist Log (NEW - ROOT CAUSE)
tested: Traced why Ask cannot answer property questions. Inspected the actual excerpt text sent to the LLM via the Ask source-chip inspector for wall Wand-010 (GlobalId 2udBPbKibCZ8zbfpJmtDTM), then located the code that builds it.
result: Failed - semantic properties excluded by design.
notes: The RAG description is built from a hardcoded 17-item English keyword whitelist (target_keys, lines 912-930) matched by substring against the lowercased property key. Three consequences. (a) Neither 'external' nor 'isexternal' is in the list, so Pset_WallCommon.IsExternal would never enter the description even on a fully English IFC - the query was unanswerable by design, independent of language, model size or hardware. (b) German fields pass only by accidental substring collision: 'Volumen' contains 'volume', which is why volumetric fields appear while Ebene, Baustoff, Dicke, Wandlaenge and Oberflaechenbereich do not. IfcOpenShell confirms ArchiCADProperties.Ebene exists on 121/121 walls (54 Aussenwaende / 67 Innenwaende). (c) Line 903 anchors the description on element.Name, which is non-unique - 22 wall names are shared across instances and Wand-023 occurs 13 times - so all 13 descriptions open identically. This is the same non-unique-identifier failure logged 2026-07-09 for ModifyAgent, but failing silently instead of returning an error. Note parser.py already persists ALL psets via get_psets(element) with no filter, so the data is in the DB and visible in the Entity Inspector; only the RAG description is filtered.
response: Recommend: replace substring whitelist with an explicit semantic mapping (Ebene->IsExternal, Tragende Funktion->LoadBearing, Baustoff->Material), add GlobalId to the description anchor on line 903, then re-embed. No schema change or re-parse required.

title: Absence Declaration Log (NEW)
tested: Tested whether the read path can state that a requested property is absent from the model, rather than answering from whatever was retrieved.
result: Failed on this model - behaviour later found inconsistent (see 2026-09-01 Duplex rows).
notes: Asked for walls with IsExternal = True; the property is absent from 121/121 walls. Correct answer is an explicit statement of absence. Instead 14 wall names were returned with no hedging. Mechanism: the LLM is never shown which property names exist on an entity - the description contains only whitelisted keys - so it cannot distinguish 'absent from the model' from 'absent from these chunks'. There is no schema-awareness channel and no instruction to verify field presence before answering. Same agreement-biased behaviour family as the RAV positive lean of section 3.3.4: an instruction-tuned model asked to answer from context will complete rather than decline. SUPERSEDED IN PART on 2026-09-01: on the Duplex control model the same question produced a correct absence declaration ('none explicitly mention the IsExternal property'). Absence declaration is therefore architecturally possible but not consistent between models - the finding is inconsistency, not a missing capability.
response: Recommend: pass the available property-key set per retrieved entity into context, and add an explicit instruction to declare absence when a requested key is not present.

title: Filter Attribution Log (NEW)
tested: Asked Ask to list walls with Pset_WallCommon.IsExternal = True. Run on reference model qwen3:14b and repeated on qwen3:1.7b. Ground truth established independently with IfcOpenShell.
result: Failed — precision 7.1%, recall 5.6%.
notes: Ground truth: Pset_WallCommon.IsExternal is MISSING on 121/121 walls; zero walls carry it. Ebene exists on 121/121 (54 Aussenwaende / 67 Innenwaende, 18 distinct external names). Ask returned 14 names; intersection with ground truth = 1 (Wand-010), and that match is likely incidental since the returned list is a contiguous numeric run (Wand-010..023). 13/14 returned names are Innenwaende. Both models returned an IDENTICAL list in IDENTICAL order at temperature 0.6, which rules out free generation: the list reflects the retrieved set, not model invention. Correct behaviour would be an explicit statement that the property is absent from the model. Recommend verifying a requested property exists on the entity before presenting it as filter-satisfying, and declaring absence rather than completing generatively.
response: Backend: does the retrieval path validate a requested property against the entity, or does it pass the retrieved set straight to synthesis?

title: Cross-Entity Quantity Attribution Log (NEW)

result: Failed — values belong to other entities.
notes: Ask reported gross 4.293 / net 10.557 for Wand-023. Ground truth: all 13 Wand-023 instances are 2.376 (Brutto = Netto = Konditionales Volumen). The value 4.293 is the NetVolume of Wand-003 and Wand-005; 10.557 is the NetVolume of Wand-015 and Wand-016. All of these appear in the retrieved source set. This also explains the physically impossible net > gross figure visible in the submitted Appendix B.1 screenshot: gross taken from one wall, net from another. Same root cause as the entity-description item: chunks contain near-identical numeric lists with no semantic or identity separator. Recommend GlobalId in every chunk and explicit flagging when a synthesis merges chunks from multiple entities.

title: Thinking Mode Log (NEW)
tested: Checked how qwen3 chain-of-thought output is handled. Ran ollama run qwen3:14b "reply with OK" and inspected /api/tags capabilities.
result: Failed — not handled.
notes: /api/tags reports capabilities ["completion","tools","thinking"]. qwen3 emits a chain-of-thought block by default: a four-word prompt produced roughly 200 thinking tokens before the answer. Castor neither suppresses thinking nor streams it as progress, so Ask presents as frozen on "Generating answer...". This contradicts §3.5.4, which states that long-running operations stream progress and that silent state changes are not permitted by design. Both models report context_length 40960, so the earlier "small context window" theory is ruled out. Recommend think=false on the Ask path, separating thinking tokens from the context budget and from user-visible output, and streaming the thinking phase as progress.
response: Backend: is thinking suppressed or stripped anywhere in the Ask path?

title: Model Switch Error Message Log (NEW)
tested: Switched the active model from qwen3:1.7b to qwen3:14b in Settings and issued an Ask query.
result: Failed — misleading error.
notes: UI returned "I encountered an error processing your question. Please check that Ollama is running and try again." In fact the server was running and /api/tags listed qwen3:14b (9.27 GB, Q4_K_M); ollama ps was empty because the model had not yet been loaded into memory. The error conflates three distinct states: server down, model missing, model loading. §3.3.2 describes an availability check with non-breaking fallback for GLM-OCR; the model selector has no equivalent. Recommend distinguishing the three states and extending the first-load timeout.
response: Backend: add an availability/load check to the model selector, mirroring the GLM-OCR pattern.

title: Read-Path Latency Log (NEW)
tested: Measured end-to-end Ask latency from LLMCallLog records (Figure A.8) rather than by stopwatch.
result: Measured — first read-path latency figures.
notes: qwen3:14b: 509,667 ms and 487,436 ms (8.5 and 8.1 minutes); a shorter run 122,067 ms. qwen3:1.7b: 210,439 ms. Record id=41: tokens_in 2050, tokens_out 605, succeeded True, provider ollama, byok False — roughly 1.2 output tokens/sec, the signature of CPU spillover. §4.2.2 reports approval latency for the write path only (T1 7.4 s / T2 22 s / T3 61 s) and no latency metric for the read path; this is the first such measurement. Hardware caveat: test machine is a Quadro RTX 3000 with 6 GB VRAM against the RTX 3080 12 GB of §4.1, and qwen3:14b ran split 59% CPU / 41% GPU. Absolute figures are not comparable to §4.2.2 and require reference hardware; the coverage gap in §4.2.2 stands regardless. Open: whether tokens_out includes the thinking block.

title: Named-Entity Retrieval Test (hypothesis REFUTED, new finding)
tested: Ask returned 'no data available for Wand-030' in a FRESH conversation and fell back to Wand-020; an earlier run fell back to Wand-023. Hypothesised that retrieval was failing to locate the named entity. Tested directly against pgvector, bypassing the LLM.
result: Hypothesis refuted - retrieval works. Separate defect found.
notes: Direct query (mxbai-embed-large, prompt 'What is the height of wall Wand-030?'): Wand-030 ranks #1. IFCEntity 790/790 indexed with embeddings, matching the Explore element counts (121 walls + 206 windows + 253 furnishing + 82 spaces + 77 doors + 26 slabs + 12 railings + 4 stairs + 2 columns + 5 storeys + site + building = 790). This also refutes the partial-indexing suspicion recorded 2026-07-09. Stored description is correct and contains the literal 'Height: 2.7'. REAL FINDING - no embedding discrimination between walls: #1 Wand-030 0.2538, #2 Wand-005 0.2545, #10 Wand-003 0.2632. Top-1 margin 0.0007; full top-10 spread 0.009. Ranking among walls is effectively arbitrary, which explains why the fallback entity varies between runs. Cause is a second-order effect of ROOT CAUSE 1: every wall description is the same sentence with different numbers, so the name token carries negligible weight in the 1024-dim vector.
response: Recommend: exact-match / GlobalId lookup ahead of vector similarity for queries naming a specific entity; and richer, semantically distinct entity descriptions so embeddings separate.

title: Delivered-Context Contradiction Log (NEW - decisive)
tested: Inspected the source-chip panel for the failed Wand-030 answer to establish whether the correct excerpt reached the model.
result: Failed - answer contradicts delivered context.
notes: The panel shows a chip for Wand-030 (GlobalId 1ZkrmZCfvDUe2ucUcWc7PF) labelled 'Excerpt sent to LLM', whose text contains 'Height: 2.7' explicitly. The returned answer was 'no data available for Wand-030'. Pipeline verified sound up to this point: indexed, described, ranked #1, and displayed as sent. This is the single clearest piece of evidence in the set - input and output contradict each other in one screenshot. Caveat: see the excerpt-count row below; whether this specific excerpt was actually dispatched depends on how the budget layer trims.

title: Excerpt Count Mismatch Log (NEW - CONFIRMED)
tested: Compared the excerpt count the UI reports against tokens_in recorded in LLMCallLog for the same call.
result: Failed - UI overstates what was sent.
notes: UI: 'Based on 32 retrieved excerpts', with every chip labelled 'Excerpt sent to LLM'. LLMCallLog id=50 (qwen3:14b, ask): tokens_in 2050, latency 293,879 ms. At roughly 180 tokens per excerpt that is about 11 excerpts. The gap holds under a conservative 100-token estimate (32 x 100 = 3,200 > 2,050), so roughly two thirds of the excerpts presented as sent were not sent. The evidence panel therefore misreports system behaviour, which matters independently of answer quality because the panel is the user's audit surface. Related but NOT proven: Wand-030 ranks #1, so if trimming is by rank it was likely among those delivered, in which case the model received 'Height: 2.7' and still answered 'no data'. Also observed: id=41 and id=50 report identical tokens_in of 2050 on different questions - worth checking whether the assembler pads or caps to a fixed size.
response: Backend: confirm trimming order, and align the UI count with what is actually dispatched.

title: Conversion Integrity Log (NEW) - PASSED
tested: Uploaded the public Duplex Apartment control model (Duplex_A_20110907_01.ifc, IFC2X3, Revit-authored) to Castor and compared the auto-converted IFC4 output against the source with IfcOpenShell.
result: PASSED - no property loss detected.
notes: Source: IFC2X3, 57 IfcWall, Pset_WallCommon on 57/57, IsExternal 23 True / 34 False, zero shared wall names. Converted (Duplex_A_20110907_01-converted.ifc): IFC4, 57 walls, IsExternal 23 True / 34 False, zero shared names. Exact preservation on the wall class. First positive result in this evaluation set, and it matters methodologically: it shows the harness distinguishes pass from fail rather than only surfacing defects. title: Whitelist Root Cause - CONFIRMED ON POSITIVE CONTROL
tested: Re-ran the IsExternal question against the Duplex control model: English psets, Revit-authored, IFC4, unique names, IsExternal populated on 57/57 walls. Prediction that it would still fail was recorded in advance.
result: Failed - prediction confirmed. Defect is in code, not data quality.
notes: Question: 'Which walls have IsExternal = True?' Ground truth 23. Answer: 'None of the walls have IsExternal = True.' Mechanism verified inside the same response: it reports LoadBearing, which IS in target_keys line 917, while IsExternal, which is NOT in the list, is absent - same pset, same entity, one key passes the whitelist and the other does not. Reproduced across two models, two authoring tools (ArchiCAD/Revit), two languages and two schema versions, which rules out data quality as the cause. Secondary defect in the same answer: walls are classified as Interior/Partition/Foundation, inferred from Revit type-name strings rather than read from any property, and presented as property status - correct for 34 of 57 by coincidence, which makes it more persuasive and more dangerous.
response: Fix is one line: add 'external'/'isexternal' to target_keys, then re-embed.

title: Universal Negative From Partial Sample (NEW - most severe)
tested: Checked whether absolute population claims are qualified by the share of the model actually retrieved.
result: Failed - unqualified universal negative.
notes: Duplex control model: 57 walls, 23 external. UI reported 30 retrieved excerpts, roughly half the population. The answer stated 'None of the walls have IsExternal = True' absolutely, with no indication that only 30 of 57 entities were examined. Element type names ARE present in context - the answer quotes 'Basic Wall:Foundation - Concrete (417mm):140479' - so type-name evidence for exterior walls was available in principle but absent from the retrieved half. Scope is wider than the whitelist defect: this affects every which/how-many query, not only queries about missing properties.
response: Recommend: surface retrieved-vs-total counts in the answer, and suppress universal claims when coverage is partial.

title: Confabulated Justification (NEW) + positive control
tested: Challenged the system with a true fact it had implicitly denied: the type 'Basic Wall:Exterior - Brick on Block' exists in the model. Then, in the same conversation, pasted deterministic IfcOpenShell output reporting 23 external walls.
result: Failed under challenge / PASSED when given data directly.
notes: Under challenge the system did not concede partial coverage. It asserted that no instance of that type is present and generated three explanations for the discrepancy (Missing Data, Filtering Issue, Naming Convention). This is the same agreement-biased behaviour family as the RAV positive lean of §3.3.4 - the model reasons in defence of a verdict it has already issued - with a direct implication: a verification layer running on the same model will rationalise rather than revise. POSITIVE CONTROL, same conversation and same model: when the IfcOpenShell output was pasted directly into the chat, the answer was correct ('23 external walls exist'). The LLM is therefore not the defect; every failure in this set originates upstream of synthesis.
response: Recommend: instruct the synthesis stage to prefer 'coverage may be incomplete' over defending a prior verdict when contradicted.

title: Read/Write Asymmetry Log (NEW - decisive)
tested: Compared how the read path and the write path resolve the SAME entity in the same session on the Duplex control model.
result: Failed on read / PASSED on write.
notes: Ask, asked about walls of type 'Basic Wall:Exterior - Brick on Block', asserted that no instance of that type is present in the model and generated three explanations for the discrepancy. Modify, given the same entity by GlobalId 2O2Fr$t4X7Zf8NOew3FLOH ('Basic Wall:Exterior - Brick on Block:143534'), resolved it immediately, classified it Tier 1 GREEN at 80% confidence, and committed the change (c2264d31). The entity's Pset_WallCommon carries ExtendToStructure, IsExternal, LoadBearing and Reference. The write path takes an explicit identifier and bypasses semantic retrieval, so it works; the read path depends on that retrieval and denies the entity exists. This is the mechanism behind the coverage asymmetry in §4.2.2 - the reported metrics measure the path that avoids the defect, and the read path has no accuracy metric at all.

title: IFC Round-Trip Integrity Log (RT-1, Tier 1) - PASSED
tested: Executed the write-back integrity test requested for the final submission: write, re-read, and confirm nothing degraded. Tier 1 GREEN property injection on the Duplex control model, with both file versions extracted from the per-project Git repository.
result: PASSED - delta confined to the targeted property.
notes: Model: Duplex_A_20110907_01-converted.ifc (IFC4, Revit-authored public buildingSMART sample). Change: Pset_WallCommon.ThermalTransmittance = 0.35 on GlobalId 2O2Fr$t4X7Zf8NOew3FLOH, confidence 80%. Baseline commit 2d25b206, change commit c2264d31, both pulled with git show from src/media/git/<project-uuid>. Compared using a GlobalId-keyed fingerprint diff (IfcOpenShell); a plain text diff is unusable because STEP entity ids are reassigned on every rewrite. ZERO DELTA in: SCHEMA; GEOMETRY (IfcFace, IfcPolyLoop, IfcCartesianPoint, IfcShapeRepresentation and 8 further classes); SPATIAL (IfcRelAggregates + IfcRelContainedInSpatialStructure containment graph); PLACEMENT (full local-placement chain per GlobalId); TYPE_COUNTS_STRICT (products and relationships); PROPERTIES_UNEXPECTED. title: Duplicate-GlobalID False Positives — ROOT CAUSE 2 (96.5% FP)
tested: Compared the Data Quality issue list for the Duplex control model against IfcOpenShell ground truth, then traced the cause in source.

In IFC4 the latter is a SUBTYPE of the former and by_type() returns subtypes, so all 56 IfcWallStandardCase instances are enumerated twice and the dedup step reports each as a duplicate of itself. No other class in this model has subtype instances and none is flagged; IfcStair and IfcStairFlight are both listed (lines 137-138) but are not in a subtype relation in IFC4, and neither is flagged — prediction holds across the file. DECISIVE: line 159 of the same file states the rule explicitly — 'by_type() returns subtypes too, so listing both would cause DUPLICATE_GUID issues' — applied to the IFC4.3 infrastructure classes but not to walls. Consequence beyond noise: the UI tells the user these elements were skipped during import; they were not, but the report says so, and this plausibly contributes to the 295 IfcProduct vs 241 indexed-items gap.

No recovery path exists: GitCommit fields are [created_at, updated_at, id, ifc_file, commit_hash, parent_hash, message, author, entities_modified, entities_added, entities_removed, diff_data, rolled_back] - author is a nullable FK with no denormalised username, and the Git layer records 'Castor <castor@local>' on every commit, so there is no second source. SECOND INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION of the rolled_back defect: f1cea365 reports rolled_back = False although a46a6b5e reverted it. COMBINED EFFECT: an auditor inspecting this record sees a change made by an unknown party that was never rolled back; the truth is the inverse - made by an unauthorised viewer and fully reverted. Two fields on one row, both wrong, in opposite directions. Bears on §2.4 and on §2.5, whose nine functional roles carry contract-tied validity windows, so account removal is a routine lifecycle path rather than an edge case. CORRECTION (12th withdrawal): an earlier note in this log claimed the audit trail does not record which user made a change. That was wrong - the application layer attributes correctly while the account exists. The accurate statement is that the chain of custody faithfully recorded an action that should never have been permitted, and then lost the attribution when the account was removed.

These are probably two different measurements - RAV verdicts on proposals versus the conflict scanner over a whole model - but both are labelled RAV in the documentation and a panel will ask which figure is current.

title: Value-Driven Clause Matching (NEW - ROOT MECHANISM, 4/4 with 2/2 controls)
tested: Probed how the RAV layer selects which requirement clause to verify a proposal against, by proposing values that match thresholds belonging to OTHER entity categories in the same brief, on a single exterior wall (Basic Wall:Exterior - Brick on Block:143590, GlobalId 2O2Fr$t4X7Zf8NOew3FLPP). Applicable clause throughout is 2.1, exterior walls, maximum 0.30 W/m2K. This trap was designed in advance when the seven-section brief was written, and the prediction is recorded there. No proposal approved.
result: Failed 4 of 4 on planted values; both controls correct.
notes: RESULTS. 0.35 -> 'Docs confirm', citing clause 2.4, foundation walls in contact with ground, maximum 0.35. 0.25 -> 'Docs confirm', citing clause 2.2, party walls between residential units, maximum 0.25. 1.60 -> 'Docs confirm', citing clause 3.3, WINDOWS including frame, maximum 1.60 - a full category crossing onto a wall. FireRating EI30 -> 'Docs confirm', citing clause 4.4, partitions enclosing a utility room with a heat-producing appliance, while clause 4.1 requires EI60 for all exterior walls. CONTROLS, both correct: 0.99 -> 'Possible conflict' citing 2.1 with correct arithmetic; 0.47 -> 'Possible conflict' citing 2.1 with correct arithmetic. Neither 0.99 nor 0.47 matches any threshold in the brief. MECHANISM: clause selection is driven by VALUE MATCH, not by entity applicability. Where the proposed value equals a threshold stated anywhere in the document, that clause is retrieved and the verdict confirms; where it matches nothing, the layer falls back to the clause that actually applies and reasons correctly. The controls are what make this a mechanism rather than an observation. CONSEQUENCE: any value appearing anywhere in the specification will be confirmed on any entity. This brief states 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 1.60 and 1.80 - all seven will pass on any wall. The defect therefore WORSENS as the specification becomes more realistic, because a longer document offers more thresholds to match against. SUPERSEDES the 2026-09-01 finding that textual comparison is reliable (R-5, EI30 against a required EI60, returned a correct conflict): that brief contained only ONE fire clause, so no competing value existed. With clause 4.4 present, the textual case fails exactly as the numeric ones do - the mechanism is value matching in general, not a numeric-comparison weakness. TWO DISTINCT FAILURE PATHS now separated: values that match a threshold produce wrong-clause selection with internally consistent reasoning (this row); values that match nothing produce the verdict/justification desynchronisation logged 2026-09-07, where 0.31 and 0.28 returned Docs confirm with arithmetically CORRECT justifications contradicting their own labels. Note also that 0.35 cited clause 2.1 on 2026-09-07 and clause 2.4 today - same value, same wall, two runs, two clauses - so clause selection is not deterministic either. UNRESOLVED CORRELATION: all four value-matching runs cited the new seven-section brief, while both controls cited the older four-clause duplex_thermal_brief.txt. Two documents are loaded; whether the fallback prefers the older one or this is coincidence is not established at n=2.
response: Recommend: scope clause retrieval to the entity's own classification before comparison, and reject any candidate clause whose subject does not match the entity type. All four cards are being used in the external expert review, because the answers look entirely correct - real entity, real clause, matching number, green verdict - and only a reviewer who cross-checks the entity name against the clause subject will catch them.

title: Verdict is an equality check, not a magnitude comparison (NEW - inverts the documented bias)
tested: Having established that V3 selects the correct clause, tested whether the verdict is derived from comparing the value against the threshold, using four values above the maximum, three below it and one exactly equal.
result: Failed - 3 of 4 compliant values flagged as conflicts.
notes: Same wall, same clause 2.1, maximum 0.30. ABOVE the maximum: 0.35, 1.60, 0.99 and 1.80 all returned Possible conflict - correct. BELOW the maximum: 0.28, 0.22 and 0.20 ALSO returned Possible conflict - incorrect, all three satisfy a maximum of 0.30. EXACTLY EQUAL: 0.30 returned Docs confirm - correct, and clause 1.2 of the brief states explicitly that a value equal to a stated maximum satisfies it. The pattern is that only an exact match confirms and everything else flags regardless of direction, which means the four correct conflicts are coincidental rather than reasoned: the layer is not testing whether 0.35 exceeds 0.30, it is testing whether 0.35 equals 0.30. The justification text shows this directly - 'The document states that exterior walls shall achieve a maximum thermal transmittance of 0.30 W/m2K, which conflicts with the proposed change to 0.22 W/m2K' asserts a conflict without performing the comparison it describes. DIRECTION INVERTS THE SUBMISSION: §3.3.4 reports a positive lean, a tendency to confirm where the layer should flag. What is measured here is over-flagging - every compliant value below a maximum is reported as a conflict. In production that means a user lowering a U-value from 0.31 to 0.22, an unambiguous improvement, is told it conflicts with the requirement. Three of four legitimate improvements would be blocked. VERDICT ACCURACY ON THIS SET: clause selection 5/5, verdict 5/8.
response: Recommend: derive the verdict from the comparison operator implied by the clause - maximum, minimum or equality - rather than from whether the value matches a stated threshold. This is narrower than the bias framing in §3.3.4 and has a specific fix.

EI30, which is below the EI60 requirement and is therefore a genuine violation: 'No relevant docs - the document excerpts do not mention anything specific about the FireRating property for wall standard cases.' TWO OPPOSITE FAILURE DIRECTIONS, which is the finding: for NUMERIC properties a non-matching value produces over-flagging - 0.28, 0.22 and 0.20 were all reported as conflicts against a 0.30 maximum they satisfy. For TEXTUAL properties a non-matching value produces under-flagging - a genuine violation is reported as having no relevant documentation. Only the exact match confirms in both cases. The consequence differs by kind: a compliant numeric improvement is blocked, while a non-compliant categorical value passes unchallenged. The second is the direction §3.3.4 describes as the positive lean, so that characterisation is reproduced for textual properties and inverted for numeric ones. RUNNING TALLY across the controlled V3 set: clause selection 6/6 correct; verdict 6/10, with three numeric false positives and one textual false negative.
response: Recommend: derive the verdict from the comparison the clause implies - maximum, minimum, or exact requirement - and treat absence of a matching value as a reason to compare rather than as absence of documentation.
